title: Becoming a Better Listener by 'Checking In' During the Conversation
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article identifies 'checking in' — periodically paraphrasing, clarifying, or summarizing what a speaker has said — as a concrete, learnable behavior for becoming a better listener. It offers specific phrasing for each mode: paraphrasing ('what I hear you saying is...'), clarifying ('is this what I'm hearing you say?'), and summarizing ('it seems like these are the three points you're making'). The piece argues checking in serves two purposes at once — it forces the listener to actually stay attuned to what's being said, and it visibly demonstrates to the speaker that they're being heard accurately. It closes by dispelling the common worry that checking in interrupts or disrupts a conversation, arguing instead that it adds energy and connection when not overused.
points: Checking in — paraphrasing, clarifying, or summarizing — is a specific, learnable listening behavior.
Paraphrasing restates what the listener believes they heard to confirm understanding.
Clarifying questions signal uncertainty and invite the speaker to correct or expand.
Summarizing distills multiple points into a shared understanding both parties can build on.
Checking in serves two purposes: it keeps the listener genuinely attuned and shows the speaker they're understood.
quotes: With this behavior, good listeners show the other party that they are indeed processing and comprehending what they are saying and that they are picking up on the intensity, emotion, tone, and conviction that colors their meaning.
Checking in involves the listener paraphrasing, clarifying, or summarizing what they are hearing from the other party.
Through clarifying questions and statements, the listener is again checking in to test their comprehension and understanding.
Checking in keeps the listener honest. They simply can’t check in if they aren’t attuned to what the other party is saying, or if they are distracted or unfocused in the conversation.
This helps both parties to gauge what conclusions have been reached together or to take stock of where things stand in the moment before moving ahead in the conversation.
